name: Morokodo
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Glottolog lists only Evans-Pritchard 1937 (classification); no grammar/phonology of Morokodo located

new_statements.quote: The reason for Baka avoiding diacritics over letters is that it was decided to mark tone in that language. There are two contrasting tones and all high tones are indicated by an acute accent over the vowel. By placing dots underneath certain letters the Baka have avoided the problem of having two sets of diacritics over the same letter. For the other three languages, although they all have two-tone systems similar to Baka, it was concluded that there was no need to indicate tone in the orthography and that context was adequate to decide the meaning in all but a few cases.
new_statements.citation: Persson, Janet. 2004. Bongo-Bagirmi languages in Sudan. Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages 9: 77-86. Khartoum/Nairobi: SIL.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (256-page OPSL 9 issue, text layer present) and extracted PDF page 90 with extracted text: printed page number 84, running head "Janet Persson". By placing dots underneath certain letters the Baka have avoided the problem of having two sets of diacr…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Morokodo is described as a two-tone (high/low) language, like Baka, Jur Mödö and Bongo; the source says nothing about word stress or accent placement. No stress statement exists in any accessible description.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Morokodo. (For Jur Mödö, the sister language sketched in the same article, tone is a syllable property with two level tones and glides on long vowels; the writer does not extend that detail to Morokodo.)
new_statements.domain_note: The tone statement is made in an orthography-survey context (whether to mark tone in the 1999 Morokodo orthography); it is a one-sentence characterisation of the whole tone system, not a word-level analysis. 'The other three languages' = Bongo, Jur Mödö and Morokodo, the non-Baka columns of the chart on pp. 81-83.
new_statements.identity_note: Persson 2004 describes the Morokodo of the Yeri/Mundri area (South Sudan) whose 1999 orthography was set by the Khartoum language committee; this is Glottolog moro1284 / ISO mgc. Glottolog lists 'Ma'di' as an alternative name of Morokodo, which is the source of the Wikipedia conflation with Ma'di [mhi] (Moru-Madi group; Blackings & Fabb 2011): the Wikipedia 'three tones' claim belongs to Ma'di, not Morokodo. Wikipedia also folds Nyamusa-Molo [nwm], Mo'da/Gberi [gbn] and Mittu [mwu] into a 'Morokodo dialect continuum'; Persson 2004 treats Morokodo as distinct from Jur Mödö and Nyamusa.

sources.quote: The reason for Baka avoiding diacritics over letters is that it was decided to mark tone in that language. There are two contrasting tones and all high tones are indicated by an acute accent over the vowel. By placing dots underneath certain letters the Baka have avoided the problem of having two sets of diacritics over the same letter. For the other three languages, although they all have two-tone systems similar to Baka, it was concluded that there was no need to indicate tone in the orthography and that context was adequate to decide the meaning in all but a few cases.
sources.locator: p. 84 (PDF page 90 of the OPSL 9 issue), section 'Comparative chart of Bongo-Baka orthographies' (chart on pp. 81-83 has columns Baka / Morokodo / Jur Mödö / Bongo, 'the four Bongo-Baka languages in Sudan which are written', p. 81)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Gives a Jur Modo phonology sketch (consonants, 9 vowels/ATR harmony, two level tones, pp. 79-80) and a comparative orthography/phoneme chart of the four written Bongo-Baka languages incl. Morokodo (pp. 81-83: Morokodo has trilled-release stops, prenasalised obstruents, lateral flap, ten vowels in two ATR sets). p. 84: Baka has two contrasting tones marked in the orthography; 'the other three languages' (Bongo, Jur Modo, Morokodo) 'all have two-tone systems similar to Baka' but do not mark tone.

No descriptive (grammar/phonology) references; only overviews/classification (Tucker & Bryan 1966, Tucker 1940, Evans-Pritchard 1937, Persson 1997, Persson 2004, Sommer 1992, Keane 1885, Moseley 2010). Alternative names Ma'di, Morocodo.

Claims 'three tones... mid, low and high' but the passage is about Ma'di and cites Blackings & Fabb 2011 A Grammar of Ma'di (Moru-Madi language mhi, not Morokodo); conflation, not usable. Nothing on stress.
